title: Théorie arithmétique. Théorie de Galois des motifs (1965) : notes manuscites (s.d.), tapuscrit (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
This page is not a Grothendieck manuscript. It is a typed (ditto/mimeograph) page from the Bourbaki internal bulletin "Tribu n° 59". It carries the draft Introduction, written by Borel, to the Bourbaki chapter "Systèmes de racines", which became Groupes et algèbres de Lie, ch. IV–VI (1968).

The text sets out the chapter's scope:
- finite sets of vectors in a Euclidean space (root systems);
- groups of linear and affine Euclidean displacements generated by reflections.

Its stated purpose is to give the natural framework for properties of semisimple Lie groups and Lie algebras over R or C, and of semisimple algebraic groups over an arbitrary field. It tells the applications-minded reader to concentrate on:
- §6, root systems, together with their vectorial and affine Weyl groups;
- in §1, only reflections of a Euclidean space or of a free Z-module;
- in §7, Theorem 1, only the implication (a) ⇒ (b) for k = R with G generated by reflections. This is evidently the Chevalley(–Shephard–Todd) theorem that the invariants of a finite reflection group form a polynomial algebra; in the published book it is ch. V §5.
- §4 (Coxeter groups), read mainly as a tool for a unified proof of the basic properties of reflection groups.

A footnote credits Jacques Tits' unpublished seminar notes for that paragraph.

Within cote 15 the page sits between Grothendieck's handwritten notes on motivic points with values in W(k), F_q, R, Z (previous page) and on discrete motivic fundamental groups via Borel–Harish-Chandra (next page). It is most likely a reused sheet of Bourbaki paper, or a stray document filed with the motives notes. There is no mathematical argument on the page itself.

One possible thematic link is speculative: Grothendieck's motivic Galois groups are expected to be (pro-)reductive, whose structure theory rests on root systems. Nothing on the page makes that link explicit.
errors: No mathematical errors; it is an expository introduction.
Minor point: the footnote says 'ce paragraphe' but is attached to the sentence about §4 (Coxeter groups), so the credit to Tits concerns the Coxeter-group section.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a Bourbaki Tribu draft introduction by Borel, essentially matching the published Lie IV–VI introduction, including the credit to Tits. Its only curiosity is archival: it is filed among Grothendieck's motivic Galois theory notes, probably as reused paper. It contains no new mathematics by Grothendieck.
